items.scene: Sam drives Lee to work every day. Lee never offers gas money, never takes a turn driving, and only asks for more rides.
items.question: Is Lee being fair in this exchange?
options: No. Lee keeps receiving help without giving back.
Yes. Lee is still being nice.
It is mainly about who is at fault for a problem.
It is mainly about how to split a new deal.
items.why_this_case_matters: Direct reciprocity check: one side repeatedly benefits without a comparable return.

items.scene: Nina pays the full fee for a shared conference ticket because she is the invited speaker, while the others attend for free under the event plan.
items.question: Is this exchange unfair?
options: No. The uneven payment is justified by the event roles and plan.
Yes. Any unequal payment is unfair.
It is mainly about apologizing for hurt feelings.
It is mainly about deciding a better bargain.
items.why_this_case_matters: Tests the shortcut that any imbalance is unfair; here the asymmetry is justified.

items.scene: Two roommates disagree about how to split a new internet bill and are choosing between 60/40 or 50/50.
items.question: What kind of issue is this?
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a deal-design problem, not a fairness judgment about an existing exchange.

items.scene: A cyclist damages a parked car, and the owner asks who caused it and whether an apology is owed.
items.question: What is the main issue here?
items.why_this_case_matters: This is about fault and repair, which is outside fairness reciprocity.
